entries.174d80ee57849c345d2868f6e0698a7c01c1a5ec: <div sID="gen32531" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="2Tim.3" sID="2Tim.3"/> <div eID="gen32531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32532" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32533" type="x-p"/> I. The apostle forewarns Timothy what the last days would be, with the reasons thereof, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.1-2Tim.3.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. Prescribes various remedies against them (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.10-2Tim.3.17">ver. 10, to the end</reference>), particularly his own example ("But thou hast fully known my doctrine," &c.) and the knowledge of the holy scriptures, which are able to make us wise unto salvation, and will be the best antidote against the corruptions of the times we live in. In this chapter Paul tells Timothy how bad others would be, and therefore how good he should be; and this use we should make of the badness of others, thereby to engage us to hold our own integrity so much the firmer.
entries.68302a454980d696e035e2ed898421ea9cf922e6: <div eID="gen32533" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32532" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Marks of Perilous Times. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32534" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come. <hi type="super">2</hi> For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, <hi type="super">3</hi> Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good, <hi type="super">4</hi> Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God; <hi type="super">5</hi> Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away. 6 For of this sort are they which creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins, led away with divers lusts, <hi type="super">7</hi> Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth. <hi type="super">8</hi> Now as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth: men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith. <hi type="super">9</hi> But they shall proceed no further: for their folly shall be manifest unto all <hi type="italic">men,</hi> as theirs also was. <div eID="gen32534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32535" type="x-p"/> Timothy must not think it strange if there were in the church bad men; for the net of the gospel was to enclose both good fish and bad, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.47-Matt.22.48">Matt. xxii. 47, 48</reference>. Jesus Christ had foretold (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.1-Matt.24.51">Matt. xxiv.</reference>) that there would come seducers, and therefore we must not be offended at it, nor think the worse of religion or the church for it. Even in gold ore there will be dross, and a great deal of chaff among the wheat when it lies on the floor. <div eID="gen32535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32536" type="x-p"/> I. Timothy must know that in the <hi type="italic">last days</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.1">v. 1</reference>), in gospel times, there would <hi type="italic">come perilous times.</hi> Though gospel times were times of reformation in many respects, let him know that even in gospel times there would be perilous times; not so much on account of persecution from without as on account of corruptions within. These would be difficult times, wherein it would be difficult for a man to keep a good conscience. He does not say, "Perilous times shall come, for both Jews and Gentiles shall be combined to root out Christianity;" but "perilous times shall come, for such as have <hi type="italic">the form of godliness</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.5">v. 5</reference>) shall be corrupt and wicked, and do a great deal of damage to the church." Two traitors within the garrison may do more hurt to it than two thousand besiegers without. Perilous times shall come, for men shall be wicked. Note, 1. Sin makes the times perilous. When there is a general corruption of manners, and of the tempers of men, this makes the times dangerous to live in; for it is hard to keep our integrity in the midst of general corruption. 2. The coming of perilous times is an evidence of the truth of scripture-predictions; if the event in this respect did not answer to the prophecy, we might be tempted to question the divinity of the Bible. 3. We are all concerned to know this, to believe and consider it, that we may not be surprised when we see the times perilous: <hi type="italic">This know also.</hi> <div eID="gen32536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32537" type="x-p"/> II. Paul tells Timothy what would be the occasion of making these times perilous, or what shall be the marks and signs whereby these times may be known, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.2">v. 2</reference>, &c. 1. Self-love will make the times perilous. Who is there who does not love himself? But this is meant of an irregular sinful self-love. Men love their carnal selves better than their spiritual selves. Men love to gratify their own lusts, and make provision for them, more than to please God and do their duty. Instead of Christian charity, which takes care for the good of others, they will mind themselves only, and prefer their own gratification before the church's edification. 2. Covetousness. Observe, Self-love brings in a long train of sins and mischiefs. When men are lovers of themselves, no good can be expected from them, as all good may be expected from those who love God with all their hearts. When covetousness generally prevails, when every man is for what he can get and for keeping what he has, this makes men dangerous to one another, and obliges every man to stand on his guard against his neighbour. 3. Pride and vain-glory. The times are perilous when men, being proud of themselves, are <hi type="italic">boasters and blasphemers,</hi> boasters before men whom they despise and look upon with scorn, and blasphemers of God and of his name. When men do not fear God they will not regard man, and so <hi type="italic">vice vers&#226;.</hi> 4. When children are disobedient to their parents, and break through the obligations which they lie under to them both in duty and gratitude, and frequently in interest, having their dependence upon them and their expectation from them, they make the times perilous; for what wickedness will those stick at who will be abusive to their own parents and rebel against them? 5. Unthankfulness and unholiness make the times perilous, and these two commonly go together. What is the reason that men are unholy and without the fear of God, but that they are unthankful for the mercies of God? Ingratitude and impiety go together; for call a man ungrateful, and you can call him by no worse name. Unthankful, and impure, defiled with fleshly lusts, which is an instance of great ingratitude to that God who has provided so well for the support of the body; we abuse his gifts, if we make them the food and fuel of our lusts. 6. The times are perilous when men will not be held by the bonds either of nature or common honesty, when they are <hi type="italic">without natural affection,</hi> and <hi type="italic">truce-breakers,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.3">v. 3</reference>. There is a natural affection due to all. Wherever there is the human nature, there should be humanity towards those of the same nature, but especially between relations. Times are perilous when children are disobedient to their parents (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.2">v. 2</reference>) and when parents are without natural affection to their children, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.3">v. 3</reference>. See what a corruption of nature sin is, how it deprives men even of that which nature has implanted in them for the support of their own kind; for the natural affection of parents to their children is that which contributes very much to the keeping up of mankind upon the earth. And those who will not be bound by natural affection, no marvel that they will not be bound by the most solemn leagues and covenants. <hi type="italic">They are truce-breakers,</hi> that make no conscience of the engagements they have laid themselves under. 7. The times are perilous when men are <hi type="italic">false accusers</hi> one of another, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">diaboloi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">devils</hi> one to another, having no regard to the good name of others, or to the religious obligations of an oath, but thinking themselves at liberty to say and do what they please, <reference osisRef="Ps.12.4">Ps. xii. 4</reference>. 8. When men have no government of themselves and their own appetites: not of their own appetites, for they are <hi type="italic">incontinent;</hi> not of their own passions, for they are <hi type="italic">fierce;</hi> when they have no rule over their own spirits, and therefore are like a city that is broken down, and has no walls; they are soon fired, upon the least provocation. 9. When that which is good and ought to be honoured is generally despised and looked upon with contempt. It is the pride of persecutors that they look with contempt upon good people, though they are more excellent than their neighbours. 10. When men are generally treacherous, wilful, and haughty, the times are perilous (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.4">v. 4</reference>)— when men are <hi type="italic">traitors, heady, high-minded.</hi> Our Saviour has foretold that the brother shall betray the brother to death and the father the child (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.21">Matt. x. 21</reference>), and those are the worst sort of traitors: those who delivered up their Bibles to persecutors were called <hi type="italic">traditores,</hi> for they betrayed the trust committed to them. When men are petulant and puffed up, behaving scornfully to all about them, and when this temper generally prevails, then the times are perilous. 11. When men are generally <hi type="italic">lovers of pleasure more than lovers of God.</hi> When there are more epicures than true Christians, then the times are bad indeed. God is to be loved above all. That is a carnal mind, and is full of enmity against him, which prefers any thing before him, especially such a sordid thing as carnal pleasure is. 12. When, notwithstanding all this, they <hi type="italic">have the form of godliness</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.5">v. 5</reference>), are called by the Christian name, baptized into the Christian faith, and make a show of religion; but, how plausible soever their form of godliness is, they deny the power of it. When they take upon them the form which should and would bring along with it the power thereof, they will put asunder what God hath joined together: they will assume the form of godliness, to take away their reproach; but they will not submit to the power of it, to take away their sin. Observe here, (1.) Men may be very bad and wicked under a profession of religion; they may be lovers of themselves, &c., yet have a form of godliness. (2.) A form of godliness is a very different thing from the power of it; men may have the one and be wholly destitute of the other; yea, they deny it, at least practically in their lives. (3.) From such good Christians must withdraw themselves. <div eID="gen32537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32538" type="x-p"/> III. Here Paul warns Timothy to take heed of certain seducers, not only that he might not be drawn away by them himself, but that he might arm those who were under his charge against their seduction. 1. He shows how industrious they were to make proselytes (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.6">v. 6</reference>): they applied themselves to particular persons, visited them in their houses, not daring to appear openly; for those that do evil hate the light, <reference osisRef="John.3.20">John iii. 20</reference>. They were not forced into houses, as good Christians often were by persecution; but they of choice crept into houses, to insinuate themselves into the affections and good opinion of people, and so to draw them over to their party. And see what sort of people those were that they gained, and made proselytes of; they were such as were weak, <hi type="italic">silly women;</hi> and such as were wicked, <hi type="italic">laden with sins, and led away with divers lusts.</hi> A foolish head and a filthy heart make persons, especially women, an easy prey to seducers. 2. He shows how far they were from coming to the knowledge of the truth, though they pretended to be <hi type="italic">ever learning,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.7">v. 7</reference>. In one sense we must all be ever learning, that is, growing in knowledge, following on to know the Lord, pressing forward; but these were sceptics, giddy and unstable, who were forward to imbibe every new notion, under pretence of advancement in knowledge, but never came to a right understanding of the truth as it is in Jesus. 3. He foretels the certain stop that should be put to their progress (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.8-2Tim.3.9">v. 8, 9</reference>), comparing them to the Egyptian magicians who withstood Moses, and who are here named, <hi type="italic">Jannes and Jambres;</hi> though the names are not to be met with in the story of the Old Testament, yet they are found in some old Jewish writers. When Moses came with a divine command to fetch Israel out of Egypt, these magicians opposed him. Thus those heretics <hi type="italic">resisted the truth</hi> and like them were men <hi type="italic">of corrupt minds,</hi> men who had their understandings perverted, biassed and prejudiced against the truth, and <hi type="italic">reprobate concerning the faith,</hi> or very far from being true Christians; <hi type="italic">but they shall proceed no further,</hi> or not much further, as some read it. Observe, (1.) Seducers seek for corners, and love obscurity; for they are afraid to appear in public, and therefore creep into houses. Further, They attack those who are the least able to defend themselves, silly and wicked women. (2.) Seducers in all ages are much alike. Their characters are the same—namely, <hi type="italic">Men of corrupt minds,</hi> &c.; their conduct is much the same—they resist the truth, as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses; and they will be alike in their disappointment. (3.) Those who resist the truth are guilty of folly, yea, of egregious folly; for <hi type="italic">magna est veritas, et prævalebit—Great is the truth, and shall prevail.</hi> (4.) Though the spirit of error may be let loose for a time, God has it in a chain. Satan can deceive the nations and the churches no further and no longer than God will permit him: <hi type="italic">Their folly shall be manifest,</hi> it shall appear that they are imposters, and every man shall abandon them.
entries.932d7c785af1e0cf603d3b70676dfa91fddf5e1e: <div eID="gen32538" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Marks of Perilous Times; Excellence of the Scriptures. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32539" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> But thou hast fully known my doctrine, manner of life, purpose, faith, longsuffering, charity, patience, <hi type="super">11</hi> Persecutions, afflictions, which came unto me at Antioch, at Iconium, at Lystra; what persecutions I endured: but out of <hi type="italic">them</hi> all the Lord delivered me. <hi type="super">12</hi> Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution. <hi type="super">13</hi> But evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived. <hi type="super">14</hi> But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned <hi type="italic">them;</hi> <hi type="super">15</hi> And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus. <hi type="super">16</hi> All scripture <hi type="italic">is</hi> given by inspiration of God, and <hi type="italic">is</hi> profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: <hi type="super">17</hi> That the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works. <div eID="gen32539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32540" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle, to confirm Timothy in that way wherein he walked, <div eID="gen32540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32541" type="x-p"/> I. Sets before him his own example, which Timothy had been an eye-witness of, having long attended Paul (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast fully known my doctrine.</hi> The more fully we know the doctrine of Christ and the apostles, the more closely we shall cleave to it; the reason why many sit loose to it is because they do not fully know it. Christ's apostles had no enemies but those who did not know them, or not know them fully; those who knew them best loved and honoured them the most. Now what is it that Timothy had so fully known in Paul? 1. The doctrine that he preached. Paul kept back nothing from his hearers, but declared to them the whole counsel of God (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.27">Acts xx. 27</reference>), so that if it were not their own fault they might fully know it. Timothy had a great advantage in being trained up under such a tutor, and being apprised of the doctrine he preached. 2. He had fully known his conversation: <hi type="italic">Thou hast fully know my doctrine, and manner of life;</hi> his manner of life was of a piece with his doctrine, and did not contradict it. He did not pull down by his living what he built up by his preaching. Those ministers are likely to do good, and leave lasting fruits of their labours, whose manner of life agrees with their doctrine; as, on the contrary, those cannot expect to profit the people at all that preach well and live ill. 3. Timothy fully knew what was the great thing that Paul had in view, both in his preaching and in his conversation: "Thou hast known <hi type="italic">my purpose,</hi> what I drive at, how far it is from any worldly, carnal, secular design, and how sincerely I aim at the glory of God and the good of the souls of men." 4. Timothy fully knew Paul's good character, which he might gather from his doctrine, manner of life, and purpose; for he gave proofs of his <hi type="italic">faith</hi> (that is, of his integrity and fidelity, or his faith in Christ, his faith concerning another world, by which Paul lived), his <hi type="italic">long-suffering</hi> towards the churches to which he preached and over which he presided, his <hi type="italic">charity</hi> towards all men, and his <hi type="italic">patience.</hi> These were graces that Paul was eminent for, and Timothy knew it. 5. He knew that he had suffered ill for doing well (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.11">v. 11</reference>): "Thou hast fully known the <hi type="italic">persecutions and afflictions that came unto me</hi>" (he mentions those only which happened to him while Timothy was with him, <hi type="italic">at Antioch, at Iconium, at Lystra</hi>); "and therefore let it be no surprise to thee if thou suffer hard things, it is no more than I have endured before." 6. He knew what care God had taken of him: <hi type="italic">Notwithstanding out of them all the Lord delivered me;</hi> as he never failed his cause, so his God never failed him. Thou hast fully known my <hi type="italic">afflictions.</hi> When we know the afflictions of good people but in part, they are a temptation to us to decline that cause which they suffer for; when we know only the hardships they undergo for Christ, we may be ready to say, "We will renounce that cause that is likely to cost us so dear in the owning of it;" but when we <hi type="italic">fully</hi> know the afflictions, not only how they suffer, but how they are supported and comforted under their sufferings, then, instead of being discouraged, we shall be animated by them, especially considering that we are told before that we must count upon such things (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">All that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution:</hi> not always alike; at that time those who professed the faith of Christ were more exposed to persecution than at other times; but at all times, more or less, those who will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution. They must expect to be despised, and that their religion will stand in the way of their preferment; those who will live godly must expect it, especially those who will live godly <hi type="italic">in Christ Jesus,</hi> that is, according to the strict rules of the Christian religion, those who will wear the livery and bear the name of the crucified Redeemer. All who will show their religion in their conversation, who will not only be godly, but live godly, let them expect persecution, especially when they are resolute in it. Observe, (1.) The apostle's life was very exemplary for three things: for his <hi type="italic">doctrine,</hi> which was according to the will of God; for his <hi type="italic">life,</hi> which was agreeable to his doctrine; and for his <hi type="italic">persecutions and sufferings.</hi> (2.) Though his life was a life of great usefulness, yet it was a life of great sufferings; and none, I believe, came nearer to their great Master for eminent services and great sufferings than Paul: he suffered almost in every place; the Holy Ghost witnessed that bonds and afflictions did abide him, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.23">Acts xx. 23</reference>. Here he mentions his persecutions and afflictions at <hi type="italic">Antioch,</hi> at <hi type="italic">Iconium,</hi> at <hi type="italic">Lystra,</hi> besides what he suffered elsewhere. (3.) The apostle mentions the Lord's delivering him out of them all, for Timothy's and our encouragement under sufferings. (4.) We have the practice and treatment of true Christians: they live godly in Jesus Christ—this is their practice; and they shall suffer persecution—this is the usage they must expect in this world. <div eID="gen32541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32542" type="x-p"/> II. He warns Timothy of the fatal end of seducers, as a reason why he should stick closely to the truth as it is in Jesus: <hi type="italic">But evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.13">v. 13</reference>. Observe, As good men, by the grace of God, grow better and better, so bad men, through the subtlety of Satan and the power of their own corruptions, grow worse and worse. The way of sin is down-hill; for such proceed from bad to worse, <hi type="italic">deceiving and being deceived.</hi> Those who deceive others do but deceive themselves; those who draw others into error run themselves into more and more mistakes, and they will find it so at last, to their cost. <div eID="gen32542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32543" type="x-p"/> III. He directs him to keep close to a good education, and particularly to what he had learned out of the holy scriptures (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.14-2Tim.3.15">v. 14, 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Continue thou in the things which thou hast learned.</hi> Note, It is not enough to learn that which is good, but we must continue in it, and persevere in it unto the end. Then are we Christ's disciples indeed, <reference osisRef="John.8.31">John viii. 31</reference>. We should not be any more <hi type="italic">children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.4.14">Eph. iv. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines; for it is a good thing that the heart be established with grace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.9">Heb. xiii. 9</reference>. And for this reason we should continue in the things we have learned from the holy scriptures; not that we ought to continue in any errors and mistakes which we may have been led into, in the time of our childhood and youth (for these, upon an impartial enquiry and full conviction, we should forsake); but this makes nothing against our continuing in those things which the holy scriptures plainly assert, and which he that runs may read. If Timothy would adhere to the truth as he had been taught it, this would arm him against the snares and insinuations of seducers. Observe, Timothy must <hi type="italic">continue in the things which he had learned and had been assured of.</hi> <div eID="gen32543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32544" type="x-p"/> 1. It is a great happiness to know the certainty of the things wherein we have been instructed (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.4">Luke i. 4</reference>); not only to know what the truths are, but to know that they are of undoubted certainty. What we have learned we must labour to be more and more assured of, that, being grounded in the truth, we may be guarded against error, for certainty in religion is of great importance and advantage: <hi type="italic">Knowing,</hi> (1.) "That thou hast had good teachers. Consider of <hi type="italic">whom thou hast learned them;</hi> not of evil men and seducers, but good men, who had themselves experienced the power of the truths they taught thee, and been ready to suffer for them, and thereby would give the fullest evidence of their belief of these truths." (2.) "Knowing especially the firm foundation upon which thou hast built, namely, that of the scripture (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">That from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures.</hi>" <div eID="gen32544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32545" type="x-p"/> 2. Those who would acquaint themselves with the things of God, and be assured of them, must know the holy scriptures, for these are the summary of divine revelation. <div eID="gen32545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32546" type="x-p"/> 3. It is a great happiness to know the holy scriptures from our childhood; and children should betimes get the knowledge of the scriptures. The age of children is the learning age; and those who would get true learning must get it out of the scriptures. <div eID="gen32546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32547" type="x-p"/> 4. The scriptures we are to know are the holy scriptures; they come from the holy God, were delivered by holy men, contain holy precepts, treat of holy things, and were designed to make us holy and to lead us in the way of holiness to happiness; being called the <hi type="italic">holy scriptures,</hi> they are by this distinguished from profane writings of all sorts, and from those that only treat morality, and common justice and honesty, but do not meddle with holiness. If we would know the holy scriptures, we must read and search them daily, as the noble Bereans did, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.11">Acts xvii. 11</reference>. They must not lie by us neglected, and seldom or never looked into. Now here observe, <div eID="gen32547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32548" type="x-p"/> (1.) What is the excellency of the scripture. It is <hi type="italic">given by inspiration of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.16">v. 16</reference>), and therefore is his word. It is a divine revelation, which we may depend upon as infallibly true. The same Spirit that breathed reason into us breathes revelation among us: <hi type="italic">For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man, but holy men spoke as they were moved or carried forth by the Holy Ghost,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.21">2 Pet. i. 21</reference>. The prophets and apostles did not speak from themselves, but what they received of the Lord that they delivered unto us. That the scripture was given by inspiration of God appears from the majesty of its style,—from the truth, purity, and sublimity, of the doctrines contained in it,—from the harmony of its several parts,—from its power and efficacy on the minds of multitudes that converse with it,—from the accomplishment of many prophecies relating to things beyond all human foresight,—and from the uncontrollable miracles that were wrought in proof of its divine original: <hi type="italic">God also bearing them witness, both with signs and wonders, and with divers miracles and gifts of the Holy Ghost, according to his own will,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.4">Heb. ii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen32548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32549" type="x-p"/> (2.) What use it will be of to us. [1.] <hi type="italic">It is able to make us wise to salvation;</hi> that is, it is a sure guide in our way to eternal life. Note, Those are wise indeed who are wise to salvation. The scriptures are able to make us truly wise, wise for our souls and another world. "To make thee wise to salvation <hi type="italic">through faith.</hi>" Observe, The scriptures will make us wise to salvation, if they be mixed with faith, and not otherwise, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.2">Heb. iv. 2</reference>. For, if we do not believe their truth and goodness, they will do us no good. [2.] It is <hi type="italic">profitable</hi> to us for all the purposes of the Christian life, <hi type="italic">for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness.</hi> It answers all the ends of divine revelation. It instructs us in that which is true, reproves us for that which is amiss, directs us in that which is good. It is of use to all, for we all need to be instructed, corrected, and reproved: it is of special use to ministers, who are to give instruction, correction, and reproof; and whence can they fetch it better than from the scripture? [3.] <hi type="italic">That the man of God may be perfect,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.17">v. 17</reference>. The Christian, the minister, is the man of God. That which finishes a man of God in this world is the scripture. By it we are <hi type="italic">thoroughly furnished for every good work.</hi> There is that in the scripture which suits every case. Whatever duty we have to do, whatever service is required from us, we may find enough in the scriptures to furnish us for it. <div eID="gen32549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32550" type="x-p"/> (3.) On the whole we here see, [1.] That the scripture has various uses, and answers divers ends and purposes: <hi type="italic">It is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction</hi> of all errors in judgment and practice, and <hi type="italic">for instruction in righteousness.</hi> [2.] The scripture is a perfect rule of faith and practice, and was designed for the man of God, the minister as well as the Christian who is devoted to God, for it is <hi type="italic">profitable for doctrine,</hi> &c. [3.] If we consult the scripture, which was given by inspiration of God, and follow its directions, we shall be made men of God, <hi type="italic">perfect, and thoroughly furnished to every good work.</hi> [4.] There is no occasion for the writings of the philosopher, nor for rabbinical fables, nor popish legends, nor unwritten traditions, to make us perfect men of God, since the scripture answers all these ends and purposes. O that we may love our Bibles more, and keep closer to them than ever! and then shall we find the benefit and advantage designed thereby, and shall at last attain the happiness therein promised and assured to us.  <chapter eID="2Tim.3"/> <div eID="gen32550" type="x-p"/>

entries.490cfd548495cf8ecce9df5983fa8f1fe4ec8838: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18212"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <div sID="gen37707" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.1-2Tim.3.17">2Ti 3:1-17</reference>. Coming Evil Days: Signs of Evil Already: Contrast in the Doctrine and Life of Paul, Which Timothy Should Follow in Accordance with His Early Training in Scripture.<div eID="gen37707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37708" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18212"/><hi type="bold">1. also--</hi>Greek, "but."<div eID="gen37708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">last days--</hi>preceding Christ's second coming (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.3">2Pe 3:3</reference>; Jude 18). "The latter times," <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1">1Ti 4:1</reference>, refer to a period not so remote as "the last days," namely, the long days of papal and Greek anti-Christianity.<div eID="gen37709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37710" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perilous--</hi>literally, "difficult times," in which it is difficult to know what is to be done: "grievous times."<div eID="gen37710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall come--</hi>Greek, "shall be imminent"; "shall come unexpectedly" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen37711" type="x-p"/>
entries.59c53868910382d95885a0e516c1376255b6a969: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18213"/><div sID="gen37712" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18213"/><hi type="bold">2. men--</hi>in the professing Church. Compare the catalogue, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.29">Ro 1:29</reference>, &c., where much the same sins are attributed to heathen men; it shall be a relapse into virtual heathendom, with all its beast-like propensities, whence the symbol of it is "a beast" (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.1">Re 13:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.12">11, 12</reference>, &c.; 17:3, 8, 11).<div eID="gen37712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37713" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covetous--</hi>Translate, "money-loving," a distinct Greek word from that for "covetous" (see on <reference osisRef="Col.3.5">Col 3:5</reference>). The cognate Greek substantive (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.10">1Ti 6:10</reference>) is so translated, "the love of money is a (Greek, not 'the') root of all evil."<div eID="gen37713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37714" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">boasters--</hi>empty boasters [Alford]; boasting of having what they have not.<div eID="gen37714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37715" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">proud--</hi>overweening: literally, showing themselves above their fellows.<div eID="gen37715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37716" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blasphemous--</hi>rather, "evil-speakers," revilers.<div eID="gen37716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37717" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">disobedient to parents--</hi>The character of the times is even to be gathered especially from the manners of the young [Bengel].<div eID="gen37717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unthankful--</hi>The obligation to gratitude is next to that of obedience to parents.<div eID="gen37718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37719" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unholy--</hi>irreligious [Alford]; inobservant of the offices of piety. <div eID="gen37719" type="x-p"/>
entries.956482e82d5850b1727442fe916b3806cf392652: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18214"/><div sID="gen37720" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18214"/><hi type="bold">3. truce-breakers--</hi>rather as the Greek is translated in <reference osisRef="Rom.1.31">Ro 1:31</reference>, "implacable."<div eID="gen37720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37721" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">false accusers--</hi>slanderers (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.11">1Ti 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.3">Tit 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen37721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37722" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">incontinent, fierce--</hi>at once both soft and hard: incontinently indulging themselves, and inhuman to others.<div eID="gen37722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">despisers, &c.--</hi>"no lovers of good" [Alford]; the opposite of "a lover of good" (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.8">Tit 1:8</reference>). <div eID="gen37723" type="x-p"/>
entries.3487927edec1626630e92998e31ee119cb790fb0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18215"/><div sID="gen37724" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18215"/><hi type="bold">4. heady--</hi>precipitate in action and in passion.<div eID="gen37724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37725" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">high-minded--</hi>literally, "puffed up" with pride, as with smoke blinding them.<div eID="gen37725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lovers of pleasure ... God--</hi>Love of pleasure destroys the love and sense of God. <div eID="gen37726" type="x-p"/>
entries.0db2a5a83ff4274943ba249de2d57143919d157d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18216"/><div sID="gen37727" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18216"/><hi type="bold">5. form--</hi>outward semblance.<div eID="gen37727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37728" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">godliness--</hi>piety.<div eID="gen37728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37729" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">denying--</hi>rather as Greek, "having denied," that is, renounced.<div eID="gen37729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the power--</hi>the living, regenerating, sanctifying influence of it.<div eID="gen37730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turn away--</hi>implying that some of such characters, forerunners of the last days, were already in the Church. <div eID="gen37731" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e9486b1b5145af0b628cc3bc110c015448f2110: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18217"/><div sID="gen37732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18217"/><hi type="bold">6. of this sort--</hi>Greek, "of these," such as were described (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.5">2Ti 3:5</reference>).<div eID="gen37732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">creep into--</hi>stealthily.<div eID="gen37733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37734" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">laden with sins--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.1.4">Is 1:4</reference>); applying to the "silly women" whose consciences are burdened with sins, and so are a ready prey to the false teachers who promise ease of conscience if they will follow them. A bad conscience leads easily to shipwreck of faith (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.19">1Ti 1:19</reference>).<div eID="gen37734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">divers lusts--</hi>not only animal lusts, but passion for change in doctrine and manner of teaching; the running after fashionable men and fashionable tenets, drawing them in the most opposite directions [Alford]. <div eID="gen37735" type="x-p"/>
entries.e00a5a49bd44be39614c23556ff906c2ee2fd6a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18218"/><div sID="gen37736" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18218"/><hi type="bold">7. Ever learning--</hi>some new point, for mere curiosity, to the disparagement of what they seemed to know before.<div eID="gen37736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37737" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the knowledge--</hi>Greek, "the perfect knowledge"; the only safeguard against further novelties. Gnosticism laid hold especially of the female sex [Estius, 1.13.3]: so Roman Jesuitism. <div eID="gen37737" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4f90f72b39fa680d41b3ea7fd9cf0deafb5dee9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18219"/><div sID="gen37738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18219"/><hi type="bold">8. Now--</hi>Greek, "But"; it is no wonder there should be now such opponents to the truth, for their prototypes existed in ancient times [Alford].<div eID="gen37738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jannes ... Jambres--</hi>traditional names of the Egyptian magicians who resisted Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.7.11">Ex 7:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.7.22">22</reference>), derived from "the unwritten teaching of the Jews" [Theodoret]. In a point so immaterial as the names, where Scripture had not recorded them, Paul takes the names which general opinion had assigned the magicians. Eusebius [Preparation of the Gospel], quotes from Numenius, "Jannes and Jambres were sacred scribes (a lower order of priests in Egypt) skilled in magic." Hiller interprets "Jannes" from the Abyssinian language a trickster, and "Jambres" a juggler" (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.8">Ac 13:8</reference>).<div eID="gen37739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">resist--</hi>"withstand," as before. They did so by trying to rival Moses' miracles. So the false teachers shall exhibit lying wonders in the last days (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.24">Mt 24:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.9">2Th 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.14">Re 13:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen37740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37741" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reprobate--</hi>incapable of testing the truth (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">Ro 1:28</reference>) [Bengel]. Alford takes passively, "not abiding the test"; rejected on being tested (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.30">Jr 6:30</reference>). <div eID="gen37741" type="x-p"/>
entries.307cf5a615f0243a607cef7c5d37011037c26d41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18220"/><div sID="gen37742" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18220"/><hi type="bold">9. they shall proceed no further--</hi>Though for a time (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.16">2Ti 2:16</reference>) "they shall advance or proceed (English Version, 'increase') unto more ungodliness," yet there is a final limit beyond which they shall not be able to "proceed further" (<reference osisRef="Job.38.11">Job 38:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.7">Re 11:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.11">11</reference>). They themselves shall "wax worse and worse" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.13">2Ti 3:13</reference>), but they shall at last be for ever prevented from seducing others. "Often malice proceeds deeper down, when it cannot extend itself" [Bengel].<div eID="gen37742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37743" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their folly--</hi>literally, "dementation": wise though they think themselves.<div eID="gen37743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall be manifest--</hi>Greek, "shall be brought forth from concealment into open day" [Bengel], (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">1Co 4:5</reference>).<div eID="gen37744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as theirs ... was--</hi>as that of those magicians was, when not only could they no longer try to rival Moses in sending boils, but the boils fell upon themselves: so as to the lice (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.18">Ex 8:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.9.11">9:11</reference>). <div eID="gen37745" type="x-p"/>
entries.864e3c2cd6ab55842fd12c75371f696207701bf4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18221"/><div sID="gen37746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18221"/><hi type="bold">10. fully known--</hi>literally, "fully followed up" and traced; namely, with a view to following me as thy pattern, so far as I follow Christ; the same Greek as in <reference osisRef="Luke.1.3">Lu 1:3</reference>, "having had perfect understanding of all things." His pious mother Eunice and grandmother Lois would recommend him to study fully Paul's Christian course as a pattern. He had not been yet the companion of Paul at the time of the apostle's persecutions in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.50">Ac 13:50</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.5">14:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.14.19">19</reference>), but is first mentioned as such <reference osisRef="Acts.16.1-Acts.16.3">Ac 16:1-3</reference>. However, he was "a disciple" already, when introduced to us in <reference osisRef="Acts.16.1-Acts.16.3">Ac 16:1-3</reference>; and as Paul calls him "my own son in the faith," he must have been converted by the apostle previously; perhaps in the visit to those parts three years before. Hence arose Timothy's knowledge of Paul's persecutions, which were the common talk of the churches in those regions about the time of his conversion. The incidental allusion to them here forms an undesigned coincidence between the history and the Epistle, indicating genuineness [Paley, Horæ Paulinæ]. A forger of Epistles from the Acts would never allude to Timothy's knowledge of persecutions, when that knowledge is not expressly mentioned in the history, but is only arrived at by indirect inference; also the omission of Derbe here, in the Epistle, is in minute accordance with the fact that in Derbe no persecution is mentioned in the history, though Derbe and Lystra are commonly mentioned together. The reason why he mentions his persecutions before Timothy became his companion, and not those subsequent, was because Timothy was familiar with the latter as an eye-witness and Paul needed not to remind him of them, but the former Timothy had traced up by seeking the information from others, especially as the date and scene of them was the date and scene of his own conversion.<div eID="gen37746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doctrine--</hi>"teaching."<div eID="gen37747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37748" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">manner of life--</hi>"conduct," "behavior."<div eID="gen37748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purpose--</hi>The Greek is elsewhere usually used of God's "purpose." But here, as in <reference osisRef="Acts.11.23">Ac 11:23</reference>, of Paul's determined "purpose of heart in cleaving unto the Lord." My set aim, or resolution, in my apostolic function, and in every action is, not my selfish gain, but the glory of God in Christ.<div eID="gen37749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">long-suffering--</hi>towards my adversaries, and the false teachers; towards brethren in bearing their infirmities; towards the unconverted, and the lapsed when penitent (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.2">2Ti 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.6">2Co 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.22">Ga 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.2">Ep 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.12">Col 3:12</reference>).<div eID="gen37750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">charity--</hi>love to all men.<div eID="gen37751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37752" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">patience--</hi>"endurance"; patient continuance in well-doing amidst adversities (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.11">2Ti 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.7">Ro 2:7</reference>). <div eID="gen37752" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3cf25d49eeb8881cd8dbb50e646d08f9b0ea67d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18222"/><div sID="gen37753" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18222"/><hi type="bold">11. afflictions--</hi>"sufferings."<div eID="gen37753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37754" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which--</hi>Greek, "such as."<div eID="gen37754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Antioch--</hi>of Pisidia (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.14">Ac 13:14</reference>, 50, 51).<div eID="gen37755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Iconium--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.14.1-Acts.14.5">Ac 14:1-5</reference>).<div eID="gen37756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lystra--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.14.6">Ac 14:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.14.19">19</reference>).<div eID="gen37757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37758" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what--</hi>How grievous.<div eID="gen37758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of ... all ... Lord delivered me--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17">2Ti 4:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.17">Psa 34:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.10">2Co 1:10</reference>). An encouragement to Timothy not to fear persecutions. <div eID="gen37759" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd860aac670781383ceda46d4591431ee3e3f745: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18223"/><div sID="gen37760" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18223"/><hi type="bold">12. Yea, and--</hi>an additional consideration for Timothy: if he wishes to live godly in Christ, he must make up his mind to encounter persecution.<div eID="gen37760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37761" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that will, &c.--</hi>Greek, "all whose will is to live," &c. So far should persecution be from being a stumbling-block to Timothy, he should consider it a mark of the pious. So the same Greek is used of the same thing, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.28">Lu 14:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.33">33</reference>, "intending (Greek, 'wishing') to build a tower ... counteth the cost."<div eID="gen37761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">live godly in Christ--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.21">Php 1:21</reference>). There is no godliness (Greek, "piously") or piety out of Christ. The world easily puts up with the mask of a religion which depends on itself, but the piety which derives its vigor directly from Christ is as odious to modern Christians as it was to the ancient Jews [Bengel].<div eID="gen37762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37763" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall suffer persecution--</hi>and will not decline it (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.11">Ga 5:11</reference>). Bishop Pearson proves the divine origination of Christianity from its success being inexplicable on the supposition of its being of human origin. The nature of its doctrine was no way likely to command success: (1) it condemns all other religions, some established for ages; (2) it enjoins precepts ungrateful to flesh and blood, the mortifying of the flesh, the love of enemies, and the bearing of the cross; (3) it enforces these seemingly unreasonable precepts by promises seemingly incredible; not good things such as afford complacency to our senses, but such as cannot be obtained till after this life, and presuppose what then seemed impossible, the resurrection; (4) it predicts to its followers what would seem sure to keep most of the world from embracing it, persecutions. <div eID="gen37763" type="x-p"/>
entries.07cf9ec2874f42a204b8f129d2fb5c0877907d52: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18224"/><div sID="gen37764" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18224"/>13. Reason why persecutions must be expected, and these becoming worse and worse as the end approaches. The breach between light and darkness, so far from being healed, shall be widened [Alford].<div eID="gen37764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">evil men--</hi>in contrast to the "godly" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.12">2Ti 3:12</reference>).<div eID="gen37765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seducers--</hi>literally, "conjurers." Magical arts prevailed at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.19">Ac 19:19</reference>), and had been renounced by many Ephesians on embracing Christianity: but now when Paul was writing to Ephesus, symptoms of a return to conjuring tricks appeared: an undesigned coincidence [Burton]. Probably sorcery will characterize the final apostasy (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.15">Re 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.23">18:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.15">22:15</reference>).<div eID="gen37766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37767" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wax worse--</hi>literally, "advance in the direction of worse" (see on <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.9">2Ti 3:9</reference>). Not contradictory to that verse: there the diffusion of the evil was spoken of; here its intensity [Alford].<div eID="gen37767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37768" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deceiving, and being deceived--</hi>He who has once begun to deceive others, is the less easily able to recover himself from error, and the more easily embraces in turn the errors of others [Bengel]. <div eID="gen37768" type="x-p"/>
entries.24a5a61534d7a755cc43caec153394a92834e0b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18225"/><div sID="gen37769" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18225"/><hi type="bold">14. But ... thou--</hi>Whatever they may do. Resuming the thread begun at <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.10">2Ti 3:10</reference>.<div eID="gen37769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">learned--</hi>from me and thy mother and grandmother (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.5">2Ti 1:5</reference>; 2:2).<div eID="gen37770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">assured of--</hi>from Scripture (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.15">2Ti 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen37771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37772" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of whom--</hi>plural, not singular, in the oldest manuscripts, "from what teachers." Not only from me, but from Lois and Eunice. <div eID="gen37772" type="x-p"/>
entries.d32c030a705cf029a2c504b2586a529aa8b86274: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18226"/><div sID="gen37773" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18226"/><hi type="bold">15. from a child--</hi>literally, "from an infant." The tender age of the first dawn of reason is that wherein the most lasting impressions of faith may be made.<div eID="gen37773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy scriptures--</hi>The Old Testament taught by his Jewish mother. An undesigned coincidence with <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.5">2Ti 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.16.1-Acts.16.3">Ac 16:1-3</reference>.<div eID="gen37774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">able--</hi>in themselves: though through men's own fault they often do not in fact make men savingly alive.<div eID="gen37775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wise unto salvation--</hi>that is, wise unto the attainment of salvation. Contrast "folly" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.9">2Ti 3:9</reference>). Wise also in extending it to others.<div eID="gen37776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37777" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through faith--</hi>as the instrument of this wisdom. Each knows divine things only as far as his own experience in himself extends. He who has not faith, has not wisdom or salvation.<div eID="gen37777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is in--</hi>that is, rests on Christ Jesus. <div eID="gen37778" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9336112549ba18a5560035f2e46bf4687b7a995: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18227"/><div sID="gen37779" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18227"/><hi type="bold">16. All scripture--</hi>Greek, "Every Scripture," that is, Scripture in its every part. However, English Version is sustained, though the Greek article be wanting, by the technical use of the term "Scripture" being so well known as not to need the article (compare Greek, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.15">Ep 3:15</reference>; 2:21). The Greek is never used of writings in general, but only of the sacred Scriptures. The position of the two Greek adjectives closely united by "and," forbids our taking the one as an epithet, the other as predicated and translated as Alford and Ellicott. "Every Scripture given by inspiration of God is also profitable." Vulgate and the best manuscripts, favor English Version. Clearly the adjectives are so closely connected that as surely as one is a predicate, the other must be so too. Alford admits his translation to be harsh, though legitimate. It is better with English Version to take it in a construction legitimate, and at the same time not harsh. The Greek, "God-inspired," is found nowhere else. Most of the New Testament books were written when Paul wrote this his latest Epistle: so he includes in the clause "All Scripture is God-inspired," not only the Old Testament, in which alone Timothy was taught when a child (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.15">2Ti 3:15</reference>), but the New Testament books according as they were recognized in the churches which had men gifted with "discerning of spirits," and so able to distinguish really inspired utterances, persons, and so their writings from spurious. Paul means, "All Scripture is God-inspired and therefore useful"; because we see no utility in any words or portion of it, it does not follow it is not God-inspired. It is useful, because God-inspired; not God-inspired, because useful. One reason for the article not being before the Greek, "Scripture," may be that, if it had, it might be supposed that it limited the sense to the hiera grammata, "Holy Scriptures" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.15">2Ti 3:15</reference>) of the Old Testament, whereas here the assertion is more general: "all Scripture" (compare Greek, <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.20">2Pe 1:20</reference>). The translation, "all Scripture that is God-inspired is also useful," would imply that there is some Scripture which is not God-inspired. But this would exclude the appropriated sense of the word "Scripture"; and who would need to be told that "all divine Scripture is useful ('profitable')?" <reference osisRef="Heb.4.13">He 4:13</reference> would, in Alford's view, have to be rendered, "All naked things are also open to the eyes of Him," &c.: so also <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.4">1Ti 4:4</reference>, which would be absurd [Tregelles, Remarks on the Prophetic Visions of the Book of Daniel]. Knapp well defines inspiration, "An extraordinary divine agency upon teachers while giving instruction, whether oral or written, by which they were taught how and what they should speak or write" (compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1">2Sa 23:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.4.25">Ac 4:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.21">2Pe 1:21</reference>). The inspiration gives the divine sanction to all the words of Scripture, though those words be the utterances of the individual writer, and only in special cases revealed directly by God (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.13">1Co 2:13</reference>). Inspiration is here predicated of the writings, "all Scripture," not of the persons. The question is not how God has done it; it is as to the word, not the men who wrote it. What we must believe is that He has done it, and that all the sacred writings are every where inspired, though not all alike matter of special revelation: and that even the very words are stamped with divine sanction, as Jesus used them (for example in the temptation and <reference osisRef="John.10.34">Joh 10:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.10.35">35</reference>), for deciding all questions of doctrine and practice. There are degrees of revelation in Scripture, but not of inspiration. The sacred writers did not even always know the full significancy of their own God-inspired words (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10">1Pe 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.12">11, 12</reference>). Verbal inspiration does not mean mechanical dictation, but all "Scripture is (so) inspired by God," that everything in it, its narratives, prophecies, citations, the whole--ideas, phrases, and words--are such as He saw fit to be there. The present condition of the text is no ground for concluding against the original text being inspired, but is a reason why we should use all critical diligence to restore the original inspired text. Again, inspiration may be accompanied by revelation or not, but it is as much needed for writing known doctrines or facts authoritatively, as for communicating new truths [Tregelles]. The omission here of the substantive verb is,' I think, designed to mark that, not only the Scripture then existing, but what was still to be written till the canon should be completed, is included as God-inspired. The Old Testament law was the schoolmaster to bring us to Christ; so it is appropriately said to be "able to make wise unto salvation through faith in Jesus Christ": the term wisdom being appropriated to a knowledge of the relations between the Old and New Testaments, and opposed to the pretended wisdom of the false teachers (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.7">1Ti 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference>).<div eID="gen37779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37780" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doctrine--</hi>Greek, "teaching," that is, teaching the ignorant dogmatic truths which they cannot otherwise know. He so uses the Old Testament, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">Ro 1:17</reference>.<div eID="gen37780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37781" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reproof--</hi>"refutation," convicting the erring of their error. Including polemical divinity. As an example of this use of the Old Testament, compare <reference osisRef="Gal.3.6">Ga 3:6</reference>, 13, 16. "Doctrine and reproof" comprehend the speculative parts of divinity. Next follow the practical: Scripture is profitable for: (1) correction (Greek, "setting one right"; compare an example, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.1-1Cor.10.10">1Co 10:1-10</reference>) and instruction (Greek, "disciplining," as a father does his child, see on <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.25">2Ti 2:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.4">Ep 6:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.5">He 12:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.11">11</reference>, or "training" by instruction, warning, example, kindnesses, promises, and chastisements; compare an example, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.13">1Co 5:13</reference>). Thus the whole science of theology is complete in Scripture. Since Paul is speaking of Scripture in general and in the notion of it, the only general reason why, in order to perfecting the godly (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.17">2Ti 3:17</reference>), it should extend to every department of revealed truth, must be that it was intended to be the complete and sufficient rule in all things touching perfection. See Article VI, Common Prayer Book.<div eID="gen37781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37782" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in--</hi>Greek, "instruction which is in righteousness," as contrasted with the "instruction" in worldly rudiments (<reference osisRef="Col.2.20">Col 2:20</reference>, 22). <div eID="gen37782" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee570d7a0b040bdc04584357815f912e63e4bb62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18228"/><div sID="gen37783" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18228"/><hi type="bold">17. man of God--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.11">1Ti 6:11</reference>).<div eID="gen37783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perfect, throughly furnished--</hi>Greek, "thoroughly perfected," and so "perfect." The man of God is perfectly accoutred out of Scripture for his work, whether he be a minister (compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.2">2Ti 4:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.16">2Ti 3:16</reference>) or a spiritual layman. No oral tradition is needed to be added. <chapter eID="2Tim.3"/>

entries.7cb8f73a0edb1d8491695a196f265b10a9fb5b8c: <div eID="gen52093" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen52094" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen52095" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen52095" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen52094" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen52096" type="x-p"/> Dangerous times in the latter days, from the apostasy and wickedness of men, of whom an affecting description is given, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.1-2Tim.3.7">2Tim 3:1-7</reference>. It shall happen to them as to Jannes and Jambres, who withstood Moses, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.8">2Tim 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.9">2Tim 3:9</reference>. The apostle speaks of his persecutions and sufferings, and shows that all those who will live a godly life must suffer persecution, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.10-2Tim.3.12">2Tim 3:10-12</reference>, because evil men and seducers will wax worse and worse, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.13">2Tim 3:13</reference>. Timothy is exhorted to continue in the truths he had received, having known the Scriptures from a child, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.14">2Tim 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.15">2Tim 3:15</reference>. All Scripture is given by Divine inspiration, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.16">2Tim 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.17">2Tim 3:17</reference>. <div eID="gen52096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52097" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen52097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52098" type="x-p"/> In the last days - This often means the days of the Messiah, and is sometimes extended in its signification to the destruction of Jerusalem, as this was properly the last days of the Jewish state. But the phrase may mean any future time, whether near or distant.
entries.11c80f379b5716b887356c1746fe1da57b8df0c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen52098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52099" type="x-p"/> For men shall be - The description in this and the following verses the Papists apply to the Protestants; the Protestants in their turn apply it to the Papists; Schoettgen to the Jews; and others to heretics in general. There have been both teachers and people in every age of the Church, and in every age of the world, to whom these words may be most legitimately applied. Both Catholics and Protestants have been lovers of their own selves, etc.; but it is probable that the apostle had some particular age in view, in which there should appear some very essential corruption of Christianity. <div eID="gen52099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52100" type="x-p"/> Lovers of their own selves - Φιλαυτοι· Selfish, studious of their own interest, and regardless of the welfare of all mankind. <div eID="gen52100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52101" type="x-p"/> Covetous - Φιλαργυροι· Lovers of money, because of the influence which riches can procure. <div eID="gen52101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52102" type="x-p"/> Boasters - Αλαζονες· Vain glorious: self-assuming; valuing themselves beyond all others. <div eID="gen52102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52103" type="x-p"/> Proud - Ὑπερηφανοι· Airy, light, trifling persons; those who love to make a show - who are all outside; from ὑπερ, above, and φαινω, to show. <div eID="gen52103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52104" type="x-p"/> Blasphemers - Βλασφημοι· Those who speak impiously of God and sacred things, and injuriously of men. <div eID="gen52104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52105" type="x-p"/> Disobedient to parents - Γονευσιν απειθεις· Headstrong children, whom their parents cannot persuade. <div eID="gen52105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52106" type="x-p"/> Unthankful - Αχαριστοι· Persons without grace, or gracefulness; who think they have a right to the services of all men, yet feel no obligation, and consequently no gratitude. <div eID="gen52106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52107" type="x-p"/> Unholy - Ανοσιοι· Without piety; having no heart reverence for God.
entries.8907d34cc96d91120ba17eeec1d7eec22f5d82c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen52107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52108" type="x-p"/> Without natural affection - Αστοργοι· Without that affection which parents bear to their young, and which the young bear to their parents. An affection which is common to every class of animals; consequently, men without it are worse than brutes. <div eID="gen52108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52109" type="x-p"/> Truce-breakers - Ασπονδοι· From α, negative, and σπονδη, a libation, because in making treaties libations both of blood and wine were poured out. The word means those who are bound by no promise, held by no engagement, obliged by no oath; persons who readily promise any thing, because they never intend to perform. <div eID="gen52109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52110" type="x-p"/> False accusers - Διαβολοι· Devils; but properly enough rendered false accusers, for this is a principal work of the devil. Slanderers; striving ever to ruin the characters of others. <div eID="gen52110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52111" type="x-p"/> Incontinent - Ακρατεις· From α, negative, and κρατος, power. Those who, having sinned away their power of self-government, want strength to govern their appetites; especially those who are slaves to uncleanness. <div eID="gen52111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52112" type="x-p"/> Fierce - Ανημεροι· From α, negative, and ἡμερος, mild or gentle. Wild, impetuous, whatever is contrary to pliability and gentleness. <div eID="gen52112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52113" type="x-p"/> Despisers of those that are good - Αφιλαγαθοι· Not lovers of good men. Here is a remarkable advantage of the Greek over the English tongue, one word of the former expressing five or six of the latter. Those who do not love the good must be radically bad themselves.
entries.98d8c3e11d8d4b4ee2ff227877c333b316bc5c7b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen52113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52114" type="x-p"/> Traitors - Προδοται· From προ, before, and διδωμι, to deliver up. Those who deliver up to an enemy the person who has put his life in their hands; such as the Scots of 1648, who delivered up into the hands of his enemies their unfortunate countryman and king, Charles the First; a stain which no lapse of ages can wipe out. <div eID="gen52114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52115" type="x-p"/> Heady - Προπετεις· From προ, forwards, and πιπτω, to fall; headstrong, precipitate, rash, inconsiderate. <div eID="gen52115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52116" type="x-p"/> High-minded - Τετυφωμενοι· From τυφος, smoke; the frivolously aspiring; those who are full of themselves, and empty of all good. <div eID="gen52116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52117" type="x-p"/> Lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God - This is nervously and beautifully expressed in the Greek, φιληδονοι μαλλον η φιλοθεοι lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God; i.e. pleasure, sensual gratification, is their god; and this they love and serve; God they do not.
entries.a9b0d1c194a88b807616bff429ceecdccb41715d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen52117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52118" type="x-p"/> Having a form of godliness - The original word μορφωσις signifies a draught, sketch, or summary, and will apply well to those who have all their religion in their creed, confession of faith, catechism, bodies of divinity, etc., while destitute of the life of God in their souls; and are not only destitute of this life, but deny that such life or power is here to be experienced or known. They have religion in their creed, but none in their hearts. And perhaps to their summary they add a decent round of religious observances. From such turn away - not only do not imitate them, but have no kind of fellowship with them; they are a dangerous people, and but seldom suspected, because their outside is fair.
entries.b4c3d6523824384519c4411dd43c68141e245071: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen52118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52119" type="x-p"/> For of this sort are they - He here refers to false teachers and their insinuating manners, practising upon weak women, who, seeing in them such a semblance of piety, entertain them with great eagerness, and at last become partakers with them in their impurities. Among the Jews there are remarkable cases of this kind on record, and not a few of them among the full fed monks of the Romish Church. But in what sect or party have not such teachers been occasionally found? yet neither Judaism, Protestantism, nor Roman Catholicism makes any provision for such men.
entries.9079bdae7d6e2ba2072f7d8f77844a7029f93960: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen52119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52120" type="x-p"/> Ever learning - From their false teachers, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth, because that teaching never leads to the truth; for, although there was a form of godliness, which gave them a sort of authority to teach, yet, as they denied the power of godliness, they never could bring their votaries to the knowledge of the saving power of Christianity. <div eID="gen52120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52121" type="x-p"/> There are many professors of Christianity still who answer the above description. They hear, repeatedly hear, it may be, good sermons; but, as they seldom meditate on what they hear, they derive little profit from the ordinances of God. They have no more grace now than they had several years ago, though hearing all the while, and perhaps not wickedly departing from the Lord. They do not meditate, they do not think, they do not reduce what they hear to practice; therefore, even under the preaching of an apostle, they could not become wise to salvation.
entries.a523936137e293f9f8dde611e8e01c860ed6852b: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen52121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52122" type="x-p"/> Now as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses - This refers to the history of the Egyptian magicians, given in Exodus 7 (see on <reference osisRef="Exo.7.11">Exo 7:11</reference> (note) and <reference osisRef="Exo.7.12">Exo 7:12</reference> (note)), and particularly the concluding observations at the end of that chapter, (note) where several things are said concerning these two men. <div eID="gen52122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52123" type="x-p"/> Men of corrupt minds - It appears as if the apostle were referring still to some Judaizing teachers who were perverting the Church with their doctrines, and loudly calling in question the authority and doctrine of the apostle. <div eID="gen52123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52124" type="x-p"/> Reprobate concerning the faith - Αδοκιμοι· Undiscerning or untried; they are base metal, unstamped; and should not pass current, because not standard. This metaphor is frequent in the sacred writings.
entries.2ed93e858b14bac62939120aab863c52285e444e: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen52124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52125" type="x-p"/> But they shall proceed no farther - Such teaching and teachers shall never be able ultimately to prevail against the truth; for the foundation of God standeth sure. <div eID="gen52125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52126" type="x-p"/> Their folly shall be manifest - As the Scriptures, which are the only rule of morals and doctrine, shall ever be preserved; so, sooner or later, all false doctrines shall be tried by them: and the folly of men, setting up their wisdom against the wisdom of God, must become manifest to all. False doctrine cannot prevail long where the sacred Scriptures are read and studied. Error prevails only where the book of God is withheld from the people. The religion that fears the Bible is not the religion of God. Is Popery or Protestantism this religion?
entries.f8156f9d3fe674b8dc40a00a23197b5aed0f8ea6: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen52126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52127" type="x-p"/> Thou hast fully known my doctrine - And having long had the opportunity of knowing me, the doctrine I preached, my conduct founded on these doctrines, the object I have in view by my preaching, my fidelity to God and to my trust, my long-suffering with those who walked disorderly, and opposed themselves to the truth, and did what they could to lessen my authority and render it suspected, my love to them and to the world in general, and my patience in all my adversities; thou art capable of judging between me and the false teachers, and canst easily discern the difference between their doctrines, conduct, motives, temper, spirit, etc., and mine.
entries.d1c42e6f81a6457caed953b47bbc66574e2dd2c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen52127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52128" type="x-p"/> Persecutions - which came unto me at Antioch - The Antioch mentioned here was Antioch in Pisidia, to which place Paul and Barnabas came in their first apostolic progress, and where Paul delivered that memorable discourse which is preserved in the 13th chapter of Acts, Acts 13:16-43. In this city, it is said, the Jews stirred up the devout and honorable women, and the chief men of the city, and raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and expelled them out of their coasts; but they shook of the dust of their feet against them, and came to Iconium, <reference osisRef="Act.13.50">Act 13:50</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.13.51">Act 13:51</reference>. Here there was an assault made both of the Gentiles and also of the Jews with their rulers, to treat them despitefully, and to stone them, and they fled unto Lystra and Derbe; and there came thither certain Jews, who persuaded the people, and having stoned Paul, drew him out of the city, supposing he had been dead. The historian informs us that his life was miraculously restored, and that he departed thence, and came to Derbe, and afterwards returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, where they had lately been so grievously persecuted. See <reference osisRef="Act.14.5">Act 14:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.14.6">Act 14:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.14.19-Act.14.21">Act 14:19-21</reference>. These are the persecutions, etc., to which the apostle alludes; and we find that he mentions them here precisely in the same order in which, according to the relation of St. Luke, they occurred. Now it is said here that Timothy fully knew all these things; and we may naturally suppose they could not be unknown to him, when it is evident he was either a native of, or resided in, those parts; for when the apostle, sometime after the above, visited Derbe and Lystra, behold, a certain disciple was there named Timotheus, well reported of by the brethren that were at Lystra and Iconium; <reference osisRef="Act.16.1">Act 16:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.16.2">Act 16:2</reference>. As these things happened in his own neighborhood, Timothy must have known them; for a person who had such a religious education as he had could not be unacquainted with these persecutions, especially as we may believe that his mother and grandmother had been converts to Christianity at that time. See several useful remarks in Dr. Paley's Horae Paulinae, on these circumstances, page 312.
entries.9dd6d713fb525bc89b7bef8d66dfe8e25f54180a: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen52128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52129" type="x-p"/> All that will live godly - So opposite to the spirit and practice of the world is the whole of Christianity, that he who gives himself entirely up to God, making the Holy Scriptures the rule of his words and actions, will be less or more reviled and persecuted. "If religion gives no quarter to vice, the vicious will give no quarter to religion and its professors."
entries.a59400b280a7f13361883134b7a412c0a39499d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen52129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52130" type="x-p"/> Evil men and seducers shall wax worse - They will yet get on for a season, deceiving themselves and deceiving others; but, by and by, their folly will become manifest to all, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.9">2Tim 3:9</reference>. The word γοητες, which we render seducers, signifies jugglers, pretenders to magical arts; probably persons dealing in false miracles, with whom the Church in all ages has been not a little disgraced.
entries.8f4ec8372c8eae852d4a8c4a883bbc92467dd4f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen52130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52131" type="x-p"/> But continue thou - No man, however well instructed in the things of God, or grounded in Divine grace, is out of the reach of temptation, apostasy, and final ruin; hence the necessity of watching unto prayer, depending upon God, continuing in the faith, and persevering unto the end.
